candidateRows: Philosophical arguments for God are unconvincing because they rest on numerous uncertain assumptions and speculative claims about divine motivations.
This supplies two foundational objections to a major affirmative category in the motion: accumulated uncertain premises and the problem of divine psychology.
After introductory biographical discussion, the debate turns to philosophical arguments for God's existence, and Fodor presents his general reasons for withholding belief.
The objection from controversial assumptions may generalize across philosophy and therefore does not by itself uniquely undermine theistic arguments.
The response challenges whether Fodor's principal methodological criticism discriminates against theism rather than supporting broad philosophical agnosticism.
Fodor's claim that theistic arguments depend on too many uncertain assumptions.
Donahue grants some force to uncertainty but asks whether the same concern applies to every substantial philosophical position and dispute.
Although uncertain assumptions are common in philosophy, theistic belief often displays an unusually large gap between tenuous arguments and strong conviction.
The answer refines the skeptical standard, connects philosophical disagreement to warranted confidence, and argues that added doctrinal claims sharply reduce credibility.
Donahue's suggestion that uncertainty about assumptions generalizes to philosophy as a whole.
Fodor concedes that the issue is not unique to religion but argues that particular arguments and traditions accumulate different quantities of controversial commitments.
An omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God's creative motivations can be grounded in moral value, making a life-permitting universe reasonably expected.
This is the affirmative's central attempt to answer the divine-psychology objection and preserve fine-tuning as evidence favoring theism.
Fodor's objection that arguments for God cannot reliably infer divine desires or reasons for acting.
Donahue narrows the discussion to fine-tuning and argues that perfect goodness supplies a bridge from valuable conscious life to divine creative choice.
Appealing to divine goodness does not make our universe probable because the account of goodness is disputed and vastly many unlike creative possibilities remain.
The response attacks the affirmative fine-tuning inference at its key probability step, arguing that theism predicts many disembodied or otherwise radically different worlds.
Donahue's proposal to ground God's creative preferences in moral value and perfect goodness.
Fodor questions both whether a greatest possible being can have reasons to create and whether any defensible morality selects a universe resembling ours.
Adding finite created goods can increase a world's value without compromising God's status as its greatest conceivable and most valuable being.
This defense supports the moral-motivation premise by reconciling maximal divine greatness with a genuinely value-adding act of creation.
Fodor's claim that creation adding value conflicts with God already being the greatest possible being.
The exchange temporarily focuses on whether a world containing God plus finite goods can be more valuable than a world containing God alone.
A quantitatively greatest conceivable being is incoherent because any proposed magnitude of value can always be exceeded by adding further goods.
The argument directly contests the coherence of a divine attribute underwriting the affirmative account of moral creation and divine psychology.
Donahue's distinction between God's greatness as a being and the greater value of a world containing created goods.
Fodor argues that merely assigning God infinite value does not establish maximal value because infinities may be compared and greater totals remain conceivable.
Even replacing maximal greatness with the omnigod hypothesis requires a contested moral theory that does not predict this embodied, physically constrained world.
This extends the divine-psychology objection beyond maximal-being semantics and argues that well-being-based goodness favors many worlds unlike ours.
Donahue's suggestion that omnipotence, omniscience, and perfect goodness suffice to model divine psychology.
After several exchanges about maximal greatness, Donahue proposes dropping that attribute and asks whether the remaining omnigod properties permit useful predictions.
Fine-tuning remains expected under theism when the laws of nature and psychophysical laws are included as background information for the comparison.
This is a direct affirmative repair of the fine-tuning likelihood argument, narrowing the relevant comparison class to worlds governed by specified laws.
Fodor's objection that theism allows too many alternative forms of life and value to predict our universe.
Donahue accepts the breadth of divine possibilities as a serious issue but argues that legitimate background information can narrow the evidential comparison.
Conditioning on our laws and psychophysical connections while withholding the constants is an arbitrary partition that does not represent the full evidence.
The objection challenges the probabilistic setup of the affirmative fine-tuning case and argues that theism's expanded possibility space weakens its prediction.
Donahue's claim that shared laws may be treated as background or cancel because they are equally likely under both hypotheses.
Following debate over how to partition background information and evidence, Fodor argues that naturalism and theism do not assign equal likelihood to the stipulated laws.
The literary beauty and cultural importance of scripture do not establish divine inspiration because no defensible baseline separates inspired from human literature.
This directly evaluates one of the stated positive cases for Christianity and supplies the principal methodological objection to it.
The claim that biblical beauty and grandeur provide evidence of divine inspiration and Christianity.
After Donahue introduces biblical beauty as a proposed Christian argument, Fodor compares parallel scriptural claims and challenges their evaluative basis.
Calling Christian experience self-authenticating does not solve the epistemic problem because it supplies no reliable way to distinguish revelation from rival experiences.
It attacks the proposed distinguishing feature of Christian experience and preserves the force of disagreement among competing religious claims.
Craig's claim that the witness of the Holy Spirit is uniquely self-authenticating and epistemically distinctive.
Donahue proposes a qualitative distinction between Christian and other religious experiences; Fodor argues that the distinction is asserted but unusable.
Belief in God may be properly basic when direct experience of divine reality is coherent and undefeated, much like ordinary trust in the external world.
This supplies a positive experiential and epistemological basis for theism independent of the success of formal philosophical arguments.
Fodor's objection that appeals to self-authenticating religious experience cannot reliably distinguish genuine revelation.
Following Fodor's criticism of self-authentication, Donahue broadens the defense to properly basic theistic belief grounded in direct experience.
Proper basicality may excuse unreflective belief but does little justificatory work once a person confronts substantial counterarguments and reflective religious disagreement.
It directly limits the pro side's principal experiential defense by distinguishing initial permission to believe from reflective justification amid disagreement.
Donahue's proposal that direct experience can make belief in God properly basic and rationally justified.
Fodor grants that context may justify an unreflective believer yet argues that informed debate requires holistic explanatory support beyond basicality.
A reburial, bereavement experiences, memory-shaping biases, and socialization can jointly explain sincere early Christian resurrection belief without a literal resurrection.
This is the con side's comprehensive alternative explanation for the historical evidence commonly offered as a central positive case for Christianity.
Minimal-facts arguments claiming that the historical evidence is best explained by Jesus literally rising from the dead.
After Donahue asks for Fodor's model, Fodor presents a multistage naturalistic account covering the empty tomb, appearances, belief development, and group persistence.
Jesus's tomb could have been intended only as a temporary nearby placement before the Sabbath, followed by transfer to a communal burial site.
The proposed temporary burial supplies the concrete mechanism by which the naturalistic model explains the empty tomb without resurrection.
The challenge that Fodor's alternative requires Jesus's body to have been stolen from Joseph's tomb.
Donahue presses the body-removal premise, and Fodor distinguishes theft from an administratively motivated temporary burial and later reburial.
Jewish expectations do not favor resurrection inference, while collective experiences and an empty tomb could produce bodily-resurrection belief under either hypothesis.
It answers a major objection to hallucination-based accounts by arguing that the relevant belief-forming evidence is shared by naturalistic and supernatural explanations.
The claim that Jewish expectations would turn hallucinations into belief in heavenly exaltation rather than an individual bodily resurrection.
Donahue argues that the disciples' Jewish context blocks resurrection belief from hallucinations; Fodor replies using collective experiences and perceived physicality.
Physical appearances of Jesus better explain both the phenomenology reported in resurrection narratives and the disciples' specifically bodily interpretation of their experiences.
This articulates the pro side's key explanatory advantage claim: actual resurrection accounts for the experienced physical character, not merely the empty tomb.
Fodor's claim that his naturalistic account and Craig's resurrection account equally explain bodily-resurrection belief.
Donahue reformulates Craig's case around appearances experienced as physically alive, contending that this phenomenology favors resurrection over hallucination.
The naturalistic model already explains perceived physical appearances, and apologists' contrary psychological assumptions about ancient disciples lack adequate supporting evidence.
This rebuts the claimed explanatory advantage of resurrection and shifts the evidential burden onto disputed assertions about first-century psychology.
Donahue's Craig-style claim that hallucinations cannot explain experiences interpreted as Jesus physically appearing alive.
Fodor says his account permits perceived physical encounters and argues that both sides extrapolate psychologically, but apologists often provide no evidence.
Extensive apparently preventable suffering is unexpected if a perfectly good and powerful God created the world to maximize morally valuable well-being.
The argument directly supports the motion's negative case by presenting worldly suffering as evidence against traditional theism and its stated creative purposes.
After the discussion turns from positive Christian arguments to objections, Fodor begins an evidential problem of evil and anticipates skeptical-theist resistance.
Divine-psychology skepticism strong enough to defeat fine-tuning reasoning would likewise undermine the problem of evil.
This objection directly tests whether the skeptical case can coherently combine its criticism of fine-tuning with an inference from evil.
The earlier claim that divine-psychology uncertainty weakens fine-tuning without defeating the argument from evil.
After the skeptical side links fine-tuning and evil through expectations about divine creation, the Christian side argues that the same epistemic restriction threatens both inferences.
The problem of evil can survive limited divine-psychology skepticism because one may know that God would avoid this world without predicting which world God would create.
The distinction preserves the skeptical argument from evil while conceding that an unrestricted rejection of divine-psychology reasoning would be self-defeating.
The Christian objection that uncertainty about divine psychology undercuts both fine-tuning and the problem of evil.
The skeptical side concedes that extreme skepticism would defeat the evil argument but maintains an asymmetry between predicting God's selected creation and excluding a deeply harmful one.
Consequential complexity gives skeptical theism a plausible defense because historical changes compound unpredictably, leaving only an omniscient mind able to compare outcomes.
This is the Christian side's principal developed defense against evidential inferences from apparently gratuitous evil in the reviewed exchange.
The skeptical claim that ordinary judgments about suffering remain reliable enough to support an argument from evil.
Having accepted part of the skeptical side's distinction, the Christian side presents a narrower skeptical-theist account based on the interconnected consequences of historical events.
Consequential uncertainty does not neutralize evil because secure moral judgments and God's broad creative freedom support the inference that an omnipotent, benevolent being could do better.
The response attacks both the moral and modal foundations of the principal skeptical-theist defense while preserving the evidential force of evil.
The consequential-complexity defense that humans cannot know whether removing apparently evil events would improve history overall.
The skeptical side accepts some uncertainty about counterfactual histories but argues that paradigmatic evils remain securely bad and that an omnipotent God had wider creative alternatives.
Skeptical theism risks conflict with ordinary morality because it is difficult to excuse God's permission of an atrocity while affirming humans had an absolute duty to prevent it.
This internal criticism sharply limits the Christian side's own skeptical-theist response by exposing a potential contradiction with foundational moral commitments.
The preceding appeal to ordinary moral judgments as a reason to reject broad skeptical-theist reasoning about historical evil.
The Christian side acknowledges that consequential complexity may be untenable if it cannot consistently preserve ordinary judgments about atrocities and duties to intervene.
Geographic religious contingency and deep Christian doctrinal disagreement are more expected under naturalism than under a God who intends to reveal beliefs and practices to humanity.
This supplies a major independent argument against Christianity based on failed revelation, historical access disparities, and persistent internal doctrinal confusion.
After concluding the evil discussion, the skeptical side introduces religious disagreement as evidence against revealed Christianity at both cross-religious and intra-Christian levels.
Christianity may answer religious disagreement by treating its likelihood as inscrutable under consequential complexity and Molinism, or by outweighing it within a cumulative case.
This is the Christian side's principal answer to a motion-level skeptical argument and identifies both an epistemic defense and an evidential-outweighing strategy.
The argument that geographic and doctrinal religious disagreement is substantially more probable on naturalism than Christianity.
The Christian side largely grants the naturalistic likelihood claim but proposes that the Christian likelihood may be unknowable and that other arguments could offset the evidence.
Appealing to inscrutable divine reasons for religious confusion is implausible and increasingly ad hoc given an omnipotent God allegedly seeking loving relationships with people.
The rebuttal challenges the main Christian defense of disagreement and unifies religious confusion and suffering as evidence against the advertised conception of God.
The Christian proposal that religious disagreement has an inscrutable likelihood under consequential complexity and a Molinist framework.
The skeptical side argues that repeated recourse to unknown constraints makes the initially maximal and loving conception of God progressively less credible.

Calling sophisticated theistic responses excuses does not refute them because human cognitive limits, historical complexity, and inaccessible counterfactuals may prevent warranted comparisons with better worlds.
This response defends the recurring Christian appeal to epistemic limitation that supports answers to both evil and religious disagreement.
The skeptical characterization of unknown divine reasons as ad hoc excuses that make the proposed God less plausible.
The Christian side argues that rhetoric about excuses leaves untouched a substantive skeptical-theist claim about humanity's inability to assess counterfactual histories and possible worlds.
Theistic appeals to cognitive limitation are applied inconsistently, since comparable uncertainty is discounted when defending cosmological and fine-tuning arguments but emphasized against evil.
The argument attacks a common epistemic principle underlying several Christian replies and contends that consistent application would undermine traditional positive arguments for God.
The Christian defense that cognitive limitations and inaccessible counterfactuals substantively justify skeptical responses to atheistic arguments.
The skeptical side shifts from the rhetoric of excuses to a consistency objection, comparing when theists accept or reject human epistemic limitations across arguments.

The general opinion of philosophers is weak evidence against theism because most philosophers lack specialist knowledge of contemporary philosophy of religion, while specialist opinion is itself distorted by selection effects.
This directly contests the expert-dissent basis for lowering Christianity's credibility and establishes the pro side's principal account of which philosophical authorities are relevant.
Fodor's claim that broad philosophical disagreement and survey results warrant substantial conciliation away from theism.

After Fodor explains that peer disagreement drives his all-things-considered probability upward from near zero, Donahue challenges the relevance of broad philosopher surveys and denies that either general or specialist polling supplies a straightforward authority-based conclusion.

Persistent disagreement among informed people still requires substantial moderation of confidence even if the exact degree is uncertain and even if many nonspecialists approach theism through considerations outside philosophy of religion.
The move defends expert disagreement as a central skeptical consideration, answers the relevance objection, and explains why very high confidence in either theism or atheism is difficult to sustain.
Donahue's contention that nonspecialist philosophers are not relevant authorities and that one must assess the religious arguments directly.

Fodor accepts that the numerical estimate is imprecise but argues that disagreement remains extensive even among relevant thinkers, that other philosophical commitments may independently bear on theism, and that conciliation should significantly constrain extreme confidence.
Peer disagreement should reduce confidence in theism, but it does not by itself support an all-things-considered probability below one-half or a justified belief that God does not exist.

This makes a pivotal concession while preserving the pro side's core conclusion, sharply distinguishing moderate theistic confidence from a skeptical probability assignment below the belief threshold.
Fodor's argument that peer disagreement warrants significant conciliation and supports his roughly ten-percent all-things-considered estimate.

Following Fodor's defense of moderation, Donahue accepts that complexity and expert disagreement rule out near certainty but disputes the direction and magnitude of the proposed update, emphasizing the importance of whether the resulting probability lies above or below one-half.

Arguments from fields such as philosophy of mind cannot settle theism in isolation because their force must be weighed against potentially countervailing arguments developed within philosophy of religion.

The move supplies the pro side's substantive reason for discounting nonspecialist dissent: worldview assessment requires comparative evaluation of evidence across fields rather than isolated disciplinary conclusions.
Fodor's claim that philosophers may reasonably reject theism because commitments such as physicalism independently rule out traditional conceptions of God.

Donahue grants that positions outside philosophy of religion can provide grounds for atheism, but argues that their proponents must also examine whether theistic arguments outweigh those grounds before their opinions become strong authority evidence on the overall question.

The same incompleteness objection applies to philosophers of religion because many relevant metaphysical, epistemological, scientific, and philosophy-of-mind considerations fall outside that specialty, making broader expert opinion epistemically relevant.
This challenges the pro side's privileged expert class and broadens the evidential base for expert dissent, directly supporting the skeptical inference from disagreement across relevant domains.
Donahue's claim that nonspecialist philosophical opinions carry little weight unless they incorporate the arguments studied in philosophy of religion.

Fodor argues that philosophy of religion covers only part of the worldview comparison, discusses the relevance of other philosophers and scientists, and presents his estimate as a rough personal synthesis whose empirical basis and expert population remain contestable.

Nonspecialist philosophers' atheistic opinions deserve little weight when those philosophers are unfamiliar with modern theistic and atheistic arguments and often rely on outdated versions of the debate.
The move reinforces the principal pro reply to broad expert dissent by offering a concrete epistemic explanation for why apparent consensus may not track the quality of current arguments.
Fodor's defense of overall philosopher surveys and his claim that other specialties and scientific expertise are relevant to assessing theism.

Donahue acknowledges specialization across philosophy but maintains that most outsiders have almost no acquaintance with contemporary religious argument, while allowing that exceptional nonspecialists can offer sophisticated objections in particular areas.

Philosophy of religion is not uniquely authoritative about God's existence because it is a disciplinary label covering only some relevant arguments, while informed work in other fields can bear equally or more directly on the issue.

This directly attacks the pro side's method of selecting experts and supports the skeptical use of interdisciplinary disagreement rather than allowing specialist religious philosophers to dominate the evidential comparison.
Donahue's assertion that most philosophers outside philosophy of religion lack enough contemporary knowledge for their disbelief to carry significant weight.

Fodor accepts that specialization limits knowledge but denies that the field's name establishes priority, arguing that expertise should instead track every issue relevant to God's existence and that no specialty possesses a comprehensive view.

Good philosophy of religion necessarily integrates metaphysics, epistemology, philosophy of mind, and other fields, yet its practitioners' theistic majority still cannot establish God's existence because selection and labeling biases preclude a simple appeal to expertise.

The move answers the reverse-specialization objection, clarifies the limited epistemic role of specialist opinion, and concludes that expert evidence supports agnosticism rather than the skeptical inference urged by Fodor.
Fodor's claim that philosophy of religion covers only selected arguments and has no privileged claim over other fields relevant to God's existence.

Donahue portrays philosophy of religion as requiring broad philosophical competence, denies that outside disputes are ignored, acknowledges bias in the specialist population, and argues that the total complexity of the evidence prevents expert opinion from settling theism in an atheistic direction.

It is inconsistent to accept that peer disagreement can force a very large reduction from extreme confidence while also claiming that the evidence is too indeterminate to support a more specific substantial update.

This exposes a claimed tension in the pro side's partial concession and presses the central skeptical demand that acknowledged expert disagreement have a determinate, materially significant effect on credence.
Donahue's position that expert disagreement should temper confidence but is too complicated to support an inference toward atheism or a determinate probability.

After Donahue recommends agnosticism on expert evidence, Fodor notes that both parties already accept a potentially orders-of-magnitude correction to extreme priors and argues that this amounts to knowing enough about the evidence to make a substantial update.

Christian claims that divine indwelling morally transforms believers generate an observable expectation that Christians should display better moral conduct than the historical and contemporary record appears to show.

The move directly advances the motion's Christian-moral-failure consideration by converting doctrines of spiritual transformation into an evidential expectation and comparing that expectation with observed conduct.

Prompted to address evil done in Christianity's name, Fodor calls it the weakest listed consideration but develops a broader test: if Christian accounts of salvation and divine action are true, believers should exhibit more moral transformation and fewer contrary fruits than are observed.
